slides.headline: Includes
slides.body: In one sentence: include.path reads another file at the point where the line stands, and includeIf.<condition>.path does so only when a condition about the current repository is true.

slides.headline: Includes
slides.body: The conditions in Git 2.55 are gitdir: and gitdir/i:, where the location of the repository's .git directory matches a glob, a pattern with wildcards.

slides.headline: Five ways the rule silently does not apply
slides.body: The curriculum's objective and the interview question count four.

slides.headline: Five ways the rule silently does not apply
slides.body: One, the trailing slash: gitdir:~/work matches only a repository whose .git directory is ~/work itself.

slides.headline: Five ways the rule silently does not apply
slides.body: Two, order: the include is read where it stands.

slides.headline: Five ways the rule silently does not apply
slides.body: Three, not in a repository: gitdir needs a .git directory.

slides.headline: Five ways the rule silently does not apply
slides.body: Four, a missing file: an include that names a file that does not exist is skipped without an error.

slides.headline: Five ways the rule silently does not apply
slides.body: Five, asking the wrong question: a scope option such as --global switches include processing off, so the usual diagnostic lies unless you add --includes.

slides.headline: Aliases
slides.body: In one sentence: an alias is a configuration value under alias.<name> that Git substitutes for the name when it is the first word of a command line, appending any further arguments.

slides.headline: Aliases
slides.body: If the value starts with !, it's handed to the shell and run from the top-level directory of the repository.

slides.headline: Aliases
slides.body: Two traps, both about arguments.

slides.headline: Aliases
slides.body: Never use aliases in scripts, hooks or CI: they exist in your configuration only.

lines.s: # ~/.gitconfig: personal Git configuration, checked on Git 2.55.0.
useConfigOnly = true # refuse to guess an identity
defaultBranch = main # unconfigured Git 2.55 still creates master
ff = only # never integrate by accident
autoSetupRemote = true # first push sets the upstream
prune = true # forget branches deleted on the server
conflictStyle = zdiff3 # show the common ancestor in conflicts
autoSquash = true # fixup! commits find their place
updateRefs = true # stacked branches move together
missingCommitsCheck = error # a deleted todo line stops the rebase
auto = 0 # avoid the MERGE_RR.lock race of Git 2.55
algorithm = histogram # moved code reads as a move
autocorrect = prompt # show the suggestion, run nothing
bareRepository = explicit # the planned Git 3.0 default
credentialsInUrl = die # refuse a token inside a remote URL
path = ~/.gitconfig-work # last, so that it wins inside ~/work/

slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: An includeIf rule that never matches. Root cause: the gitdir pattern has no trailing slash, so it matches only a .git directory at exactly that path.
The rule matches and the wrong value still wins. Root cause: the [user] section stands after the include in the file, and the value read last wins.
git config get --global user.email shows the "wrong" address. Root cause: naming a scope switches include processing off; add --includes, or ask without a scope inside the repository.
A shell alias receives its argument twice. Root cause: Git runs the alias with "$@" appended; wrap the body in a function that consumes the arguments.

This video is about configuration that depends on where you are, about settings you should choose on purpose, and about the tools that make Git say what it is doing. Keep that missing slash in mind. beats.text: A team file, opted into. Git never reads configuration from the files it tracks. If it did, cloning a repository would let its author set your pager, your SSH command and your hooks. So a team that wants shared settings commits a file and asks each member to include it once. Review changes to such a file like code: it can define an alias that runs a shell command.

beats.text: The settings to decide deliberately. The textbook lists twenty settings in a table with six columns: what it does, why it matters, its downside, whether it is optional, and whether it is personal or a team matter. Read the downside column aloud for the seven kinds this video's objective names.

beats.text: pull.rebase: how git pull integrates. With nothing set, a diverged pull is fatal. Downside of true: it gives unpublished commits new IDs and flattens local merges. pull.ff=only: pull refuses anything but a fast-forward. In configuration it wins over pull.rebase, so a diverged pull needs a flag.

Downside of `true`: it gives unpublished commits new IDs and flattens local merges. `pull.ff=only`: pull refuses anything but a fast-forward. In configuration it wins over `pull.rebase`, so a diverged pull needs a flag.

beats.text: push.autoSetupRemote, which the textbook dates to Git 2.37: the first push of a branch sets its upstream. Downside: a mistyped branch name is published at once. push.default: leave the default, simple.

beats.text: Aliases. In one sentence: an alias is a configuration value under alias.<name> that Git substitutes for the name when it is the first word of a command line, appending any further arguments.
beats.tele: Aliases. In one sentence: an alias is a configuration value under `alias.<name>` that Git substitutes for the name when it is the first word of a command line, appending any further arguments.

beats.text: If the value starts with !, it's handed to the shell and run from the top-level directory of the repository. Otherwise it's a Git command line. An alias can't replace an existing command. Defining one is git config set, which is 🟡 CAUTION.
beats.tele: If the value starts with `!`, it's handed to the shell and run from the top-level directory of the repository. Otherwise it's a Git command line. An alias can't replace an existing command. Defining one is `git config set`, which is 🟡 CAUTION.

beats.text: Two traps, both about arguments. Arguments after the alias name are appended to the expansion. And for a shell alias, Git runs sh -c with the alias and "$@": the arguments are available as $1, and are also appended. The manual's remedy is a function that consumes them.
beats.tele: Two traps, both about arguments. Arguments after the alias name are appended to the expansion. And for a shell alias, Git runs `sh -c` with the alias and `"$@"`: the arguments are available as `$1`, and are also appended. The manual's remedy is a function that consumes them.

beats.text: Never use aliases in scripts, hooks or CI: they exist in your configuration only.
beats.tele: Never use aliases in scripts, hooks or CI: they exist in your configuration only.

beats.text: Environment variables for diagnosis. Configuration says what Git should do. These variables make Git say what it is doing.
beats.tele: Environment variables for diagnosis. Configuration says what Git should do. These variables make Git say what it is doing.

beats.text: GIT_TRACE=1: alias expansion, and the built-in and external commands that are started. GIT_TRACE_SETUP=1: the .git directory, the working tree, the current directory and prefix Git settled on. Use it when Git picks up the wrong repository, or none. GIT_TRACE_PACKET=1: the protocol conversation with a remote. GIT_TRACE_CURL=1: the HTTP exchange. GIT_SSH_COMMAND: replaces the ssh program and its options for this command. GIT_TRACE2_PERF=1: timings inside a command. A value of 1, 2 or true writes to standard error, and an absolute path appends to that file.
beats.tele: `GIT_TRACE=1`: alias expansion, and the built-in and external commands that are started. `GIT_TRACE_SETUP=1`: the `.git` directory, the working tree, the current directory and prefix Git settled on. Use it when Git picks up the wrong repository, or none. `GIT_TRACE_PACKET=1`: the protocol conversation with a remote. `GIT_TRACE_CURL=1`: the HTTP exchange. `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`: replaces the `ssh` program and its options for this command. `GIT_TRACE2_PERF=1`: timings inside a command. A value of `1`, `2` or `true` writes to standard error, and an absolute path appends to that file.

beats.text: The HTTP variables need a server, so they are not run here. The textbook's version note: older tutorials name GIT_CURL_VERBOSE. The Git 2.55 manual documents GIT_TRACE_CURL. Since which release is not established. Keep GIT_TRACE_REDACT at its default, so that Authorization headers stay out of the output you paste into a ticket.
